analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-run prescription drug plan that negotiates lower drug prices for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in November 2003 and referred to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Weeks after the 2003 Medicare law created a new prescription drug benefit run entirely through private insurers, this bill would have added a government-run alternative. Medicare itself would offer one national standard drug plan and negotiate prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, aiming to cut what seniors pay. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would gain access to a single nationally uniform drug plan with prices negotiated by the government rather than set by private insurers, potentially lowering premiums and out-of-pocket drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2006, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have to offer a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan available in every state, offering standard drug coverage and access to negotiated prices [S3].

The Secretary would be required to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered Medicare Part D drugs and to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents, using strategies similar to those of other federal drug purchasers [S3].
The plan's monthly premium would be uniform nationwide and set by the Secretary based on the plan's estimated actuarial cost, so seniors in every region would pay the same [S3].
In areas where private plans fail to offer drug coverage, the Secretary could designate the Medicare-run plan as the fallback plan available to beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose negotiated sale prices to the Medicare plan would be lower than current market prices, and private insurers offering competing Part D drug plans, who would face a government-run competitor.

drawbacks.text: The bill limits the government plan to standard coverage with no supplemental benefits, so beneficiaries wanting richer coverage would still need private plans [S3].

Government price negotiation can reduce drug company revenues, an objection the industry has long argued could slow investment in new medicines; the bill counters this only by requiring that cheaper alternatives not override medical necessity as determined by the prescribing physician [S3].

Running a national drug plan creates new administrative responsibilities for Medicare, though the bill requires the premium to account for administrative expenses comparable to those of private plans [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is lower drug prices for seniors against lower revenues for drug makers and competition for private insurers. The bill preserved physician discretion over prescriptions and let beneficiaries keep private options, so its main cost falls on industry rather than on patients. It never received any committee or floor consideration, so its real-world design questions were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on November 24, 2003, amending the brand-new Medicare Part D drug benefit created by the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which had jurisdiction over Medicare [S1].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor debate — before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 [S1].
The bill was written to add a government-run option on top of the Part D structure the 2003 law had just created, which had barred the government from negotiating drug prices [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private insurers, who kept the 2003 Medicare drug law's structure intact: prices set without government negotiation and coverage delivered entirely through private plans. Medicare beneficiaries did not get the negotiated-price public option.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters on record were Democrats, and no Republicans sponsored the bill; the underlying 2003 Medicare drug law it sought to amend had passed largely along party lines.

industries.note: A Medicare-run plan required to negotiate drug prices would push manufacturers' prices below what private plans pay. That saving would flow to beneficiaries through lower premiums and drug costs.

The bill creates a government-run competitor available nationwide in every Part D region, which could draw enrollment away from private drug plans and could be designated the fallback plan where private plans are absent.
